stories.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel son of Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Mar Yehuda met the two sages at the entrance of Rabba's study hall and posed a contradiction between two baraitot about Rabbi Shimon's view.
stories.turn: The two sages could not answer and fell silent.
stories.outcome: They went to Rabba, who dismissed the questioner as quarrelsome and resolved the contradiction.
stories.summary: Mar Yehuda found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel standing at Rabba's study hall and challenged them with two conflicting teachings of Rabbi Shimon. They had no answer and were silent. They brought the question to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and explained that the first teaching concerned an animal found to be a tereifa.

stories.actor: Ulla and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Ulla, who often went up to Eretz Yisrael, died outside the land.
stories.turn: Told his coffin was being brought to the land, Rabbi Elazar said burial after death is not like being absorbed by the land while alive.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar lamented him as one who died in an unclean land.
stories.summary: Ulla used to travel to Eretz Yisrael but died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar heard, he lamented that the verse about dying in an unclean land was fulfilled in him. Told that Ulla's coffin was coming for burial, he replied that being received by the land after death is not like being received while alive.

stories.actor: A man from Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Hanina
stories.event: A man whose brother died childless asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go down to Babylonia to perform levirate marriage with the widow.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hanina condemned the dead brother for leaving the land and marrying abroad.
stories.outcome: He told the man, in effect, not to follow his brother out of the land.
stories.summary: A man's brother had died leaving a widow in Bei Hoza'a in Babylonia, and the man asked Rabbi Hanina whether he might go down to marry her. Rabbi Hanina answered that the brother had married a 'Samaritan' and died, blessed be God who killed him, and asked whether the man now wanted to follow him down.

stories.actor: A man who left Pumbedita for Astonia
stories.event: A man left Pumbedita to live in Astonia, beyond Babylonia's borders.
stories.turn: He died there.
stories.outcome: Abaye said that had he wanted, he would still be alive.
stories.summary: A scholar left Pumbedita for Astonia, outside Babylonia proper, and died. Abaye remarked that had he wished, he could have stayed and still be alive.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his wife
stories.event: Mar Ukva secretly left four dinars daily in a poor neighbor's door, and one day the poor man went out to discover his benefactor.
stories.turn: Fleeing into a still-hot furnace, Mar Ukva's legs were burned while his wife's were not, and he was distressed.
stories.outcome: His wife explained that her charity was greater because she gave food directly at home.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to slip four dinars daily into a poor neighbor's door. One day the poor man resolved to see who it was; Mar Ukva and his wife, delayed that day, were spotted and ran into a raked-out furnace to avoid being identified. His legs were scorched but hers were not, and when he grew upset she explained that her giving, ready food at home, was more immediate than his.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his son
stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his annual 400 dinars to a poor neighbor by his son, who returned saying the man did not need it since they sprinkled old wine for him.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva concluded the man was so pampered that he needed more.
stories.outcome: He doubled the sum and sent it.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva sent a poor neighbor 400 dinars every Yom Kippur eve. One year his son brought it back, saying he had seen old wine poured out to perfume the man's room. Mar Ukva said that if he was that pampered he needed more, and doubled the gift.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He judged it too little provision for the long journey ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his remaining wealth.
stories.summary: As he was dying, Mar Ukva reviewed his charity accounts and saw seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the way far, he rose and distributed half his fortune to charity.

stories.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil and Shmuel
stories.event: Rav Yosef issued a practical ruling following Rav's opinion against Shmuel's.
stories.turn: Shmuel took offense.
stories.outcome: Shmuel sarcastically remarked that wisdom must have been measured out to this scholar in a large measure.
stories.summary: Rav Yosef of Dabil decided an actual case in accordance with Rav's view on a father's betrothal of a daughter who had come of age. Shmuel was offended and asked sarcastically whether everyone else got wisdom in a small measure and this man in a large one.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish, Rav Hiyya bar Abba, and Yehuda bar Nahmani
stories.event: When the child of Rav Hiyya bar Abba, his children's teacher, died, Reish Lakish came the next day with his disseminator to comfort him.
stories.turn: The disseminator's first words seemed to blame the death on the father's sins, troubling the mourner.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish had him go on to speak praises of God and words of comfort for the mourners, the comforters, and all Israel.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya bar Abba, who taught Reish Lakish's sons, lost a child. Reish Lakish did not visit the first day but came the next with his disseminator Yehuda bar Nahmani and asked him to speak about the child; he opened with a verse about children dying for their fathers' provocation (or, some say, about young men). Reish Lakish then had him speak in praise of God, to the mourners, to those who comfort them, and for all Israel, each ending in a blessing.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel
stories.event: Funerals had become so costly that relatives would abandon their dead and flee.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel instructed that he be buried simply in linen garments.
stories.outcome: All the people followed his example, and simple burial became the norm.
stories.summary: Burial expenses had grown so heavy that families sometimes abandoned the corpse. Rabban Gamliel set an example of humility by having himself buried in plain linen, and everyone followed him; Rav Pappa notes people now use even cheap rough cloth.

stories.actor: A widow's son, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
stories.event: A widow's son asked whether father or mother should be served water first, and both sages answered the father.
stories.turn: He then asked about a divorced mother, and Rabbi Yehoshua saw from his tearful eyes that he was a widow's son asking irrelevantly.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua mockingly told him to pour water in a basin and cluck at them like chickens.
stories.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer whom to serve first if both parents asked for water, and was told the father; Rabbi Yehoshua said the same. When he pressed with a question about a divorced mother, Rabbi Yehoshua said his tear-filled eyes showed he was a widow's son, and answered sarcastically that he should put water in a bowl and call them like chickens.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina
stories.event: The Sages wanted to buy merchandise from Dama ben Netina of Ashkelon at a profit of six hundred thousand.
stories.turn: The key was under his sleeping father's head.
stories.outcome: He did not wake his father, forgoing the deal.
stories.summary: Asked how far honoring parents extends, Rav Ulla told of the gentile Dama ben Netina of Ashkelon. Sages sought to buy goods from him for a huge profit, but the key lay under his sleeping father's pillow, and he would not disturb his father.

stories.actor: A man and Rabban Gamliel
stories.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he found his bride's orifice unobstructed.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he may have entered at an angle (or deliberately) and so found no obstruction.
stories.outcome: He illustrated with a parable of a man finding a door open or locked in the dark.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel claiming his bride was not a virgin because he met no obstruction. Rabban Gamliel suggested that he had perhaps diverted his approach, comparing it to a man in the dark who finds a door open only if he moves the bolt; some say he suggested the man did so deliberately.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, while the bride insisted she had been a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel had the cloth soaked and laundered, revealing drops of blood.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: A man told Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi that he had found no blood, and his bride said she had been a virgin. Rabban Gamliel had the sheet brought, soaked and washed, and blood drops appeared. He told the groom she was a virgin and to accept his bride.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, and the bride said she was still a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel tested two maidservants on a wine barrel to verify the method, then tested the bride, and no scent diffused from her.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: Another groom came to Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi claiming no blood, while his bride said she was still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel seated a virgin and a non-virgin maidservant over a wine barrel and found the wine's scent rose only from the non-virgin. He then seated the bride, no scent rose, and he told the groom to accept her.

stories.actor: An unmarried man and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A man who had never been married told Rav Nahman he found his bride's orifice unobstructed.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman inferred that his experience must have come from prostitutes.
stories.outcome: He ordered him flogged with palm branches.
stories.summary: A bachelor came to Rav Nahman claiming his bride was not a virgin because he met no obstruction. Rav Nahman reasoned he could only know this from experience with prostitutes and ordered him flogged with palm branches.

stories.actor: A man and Rabban Gamliel
stories.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he found his bride's orifice unobstructed.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he may have entered at an angle (or deliberately).
stories.outcome: He illustrated with a parable of a door found open or locked in the dark.
stories.summary: A man claimed before Rabban Gamliel that his bride was not a virgin. Rabban Gamliel suggested he had perhaps diverted his approach, comparing it to someone in the dark who finds a door open only if he moves the bolt; some say he suggested it was deliberate.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, while the bride insisted she had been a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel had the cloth soaked and laundered, revealing drops of blood.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: A man told Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi he had found no blood, and the bride said she had been a virgin. The cloth was brought, soaked and washed, and drops of blood appeared, so Rabban Gamliel told the groom to accept his bride.

stories.actor: Rav Ika bar Avin, Abaye and Rav Hananel
stories.event: Rav Ika bar Avin reported in Rav's name that Hillazon Nihavnad has unflawed lineage.
stories.turn: Abaye accused him of bias because a yevama from there had fallen to him, and Rav Ika insisted the teaching was Rav Hananel's.
stories.outcome: They asked Rav Hananel, who confirmed the teaching in Rav's name.
stories.summary: Rav Ika bar Avin taught that Hillazon Nihavnad is like Babylonia for lineage. Abaye told people not to listen, since Rav Ika had a yevama from there and wanted to marry her. Rav Ika answered that the statement was Rav Hananel's, and when they asked Rav Hananel he confirmed it in Rav's name.

stories.actor: Rav Nahman, his relative and her daughter
stories.event: Rav Nahman's relative sold her marriage-contract rights, then was divorced and died, and the buyers claimed from her daughter.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman publicly hinted that the daughter could forgive the debt to her father and inherit it; she heard and did so.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman regretted it, saying he had acted like an advocate rather than a judge.
stories.summary: A relative of Rav Nahman sold her rights in her marriage contract, then was divorced and died, and the buyers came to collect from her daughter. Rav Nahman wondered aloud whether no one would advise her to forgive the contract to her father and later inherit it; the daughter heard and did it. Afterwards Rav Nahman said with regret that he had made himself like a lawyer for litigants.

stories.actor: A woman of Mehoza and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A woman from Mehoza married to a man of Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract.
stories.turn: He recognized her Mehoza accent and ruled by Rav's custom, but was told she was marrying into Neharde'a.
stories.outcome: He reversed and applied Shmuel's custom, as practiced in Neharde'a.
stories.summary: A woman from Mehoza who was married to a man from Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman. Recognizing her accent, he said Babylonia follows Rav. When they pointed out she had married into Neharde'a, he said that in that case Neharde'a follows Shmuel.

stories.actor: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan
stories.event: Traveling outside Eretz Yisrael, the two saw a man sowing mixed seeds and then a man sowing wheat and barley among vines.
stories.turn: Each time one proposed excommunicating the man, and the other said he did not understand these laws.
stories.outcome: The men were not excommunicated, since outside the land and short of sowing all three together it was not forbidden.
stories.summary: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan were on the road and saw a man planting diverse seeds together; one wanted to excommunicate him, and the other said he did not understand the law. They then saw a man sowing wheat and barley among vines, and again the other refused, citing Rabbi Yoshiya's view that liability requires sowing wheat, barley and a grape seed in one motion.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his son
stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his annual 400 dinars to a poor neighbor by his son, who reported that the man had old wine sprinkled for him.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva concluded the man was pampered and needed more.
stories.outcome: He doubled the sum and sent it.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to send a poor neighbor 400 dinars every Yom Kippur eve. His son came back saying the man did not need it, since old wine was spilled to perfume his house. Mar Ukva said someone that pampered needs more, and doubled the gift.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: Dying, Mar Ukva reviewed his charity records and found seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He felt his provisions too light for the long journey.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his wealth.
stories.summary: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity accounts and saw he had given seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the way long, he gave away half his remaining money.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina and his wife
stories.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars to a poor man via his wife, who returned saying he did not need it.
stories.turn: She had overheard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hanina cited Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, who excuse our failures toward the truly poor.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina sent a poor man four dinars every Friday. Once his wife took it and came back saying the man was not needy: she had heard them ask him whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina quoted Rabbi Elazar that we should appreciate swindlers, for without them we would be sinning daily.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized an orphans' cow for a debt, and he approved.
stories.turn: Reish Lakish told them to return it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he could do nothing, since his equal disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan seized a cow belonging to orphans as payment of their father's debt, and Rabbi Yohanan told them they had done well. Reish Lakish ordered them to give it back. When they returned to Rabbi Yohanan, he said there was nothing he could do, since an equal of his disagreed.

stories.actor: A creditor, the orphans' herdsman and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, claiming he took it while the debtor was alive; the herdsman said it was after death.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman found the herdsman had no witnesses to the seizure.
stories.outcome: He ruled the creditor was believed, since he could have claimed he bought it.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans, saying he seized it during their father's lifetime; the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman asked whether there were witnesses to the seizure, and when there were none he believed the creditor, since he could equally have claimed he had bought it.

stories.actor: The house of the Nasi, Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: The Nasi's household seized an orphans' maidservant for a debt, and Rabbi Abbahu's court approved.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abba accused the judges of flattering the Nasi's house and cited Reish Lakish's reversal of such a ruling.
stories.outcome: The window ends with Rabbi Abba's challenge.
stories.summary: Members of the Nasi's household seized a maidservant belonging to orphans as payment, and Rabbi Abbahu, sitting with other judges, said they had done well. Rabbi Abba, sitting with them, asked whether they were flattering the Nasi's house, reminding them that Reish Lakish had reversed a ruling made according to Rabbi Tarfon.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya bar Adda and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rav Hiyya bar Adda missed three days of teaching children, and Reish Lakish asked why.
stories.turn: He explained he was harvesting a vine his father left him, whose yield declined each day.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish told him that had he not neglected teaching, it would have yielded more.
stories.summary: The schoolteacher Rav Hiyya bar Adda stayed away for three days. He told Reish Lakish he had been harvesting a single vine branch his father left him, three hundred clusters a day, though each day it took more clusters to fill a jug, and he had abandoned more than half. Reish Lakish said that had he not missed teaching, the vine would have produced even more.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina
stories.event: Visiting a certain place, the sages were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot.
stories.turn: It was too large for them to finish.
stories.outcome: They ate a third, declared a third ownerless, and gave a third to their animals.
stories.summary: Three sages came to a place where they were brought a peach as large as a Kefar Hino stewpot, which held five se'a. They ate one third, left one third ownerless, and fed the rest to their animals.

stories.actor: A man who made a conditional divorce
stories.event: A man said his bill of divorce would take effect if he did not return within thirty days, and arrived at the end of the period.
stories.turn: The ferry was on the other side and he could not cross, though he shouted that he had come.
stories.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this did not count as returning.
stories.summary: A man set a condition that a divorce take effect if he was not back within thirty days. He arrived on the last day but was stranded because the ferry was on the far bank, and he called out 'See, I have come.' Shmuel ruled that this was not a return.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, so he made himself covered in boils by incantation, but she healed him by magic.
stories.turn: He fled and hid in a demon-haunted bathhouse.
stories.outcome: He survived, guarded by angels all night, and the Sages explained it as a miracle for resisting sin.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi; he used a spell to cover himself with sores, but she cured him with sorcery. He escaped into a bathhouse so dangerous that even pairs were harmed there by day. The next day he told the Sages that two royal guards protected him all night, and they said it was a miracle for one who escaped forbidden relations.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok, and he asked for food, accepting non-kosher food as no worse.
stories.turn: When she lit the oven, he climbed in and sat inside it.
stories.outcome: She said that had she known how seriously he took it, she would not have troubled him.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Tzadok. He said he was weak and asked for food; she offered something non-kosher and he said one who does the first eats the second. When she heated the oven he climbed in, explaining that whoever does such a deed falls into such a fire, and she said she would not have pressed him had she known.

stories.actor: Rav Kahana
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, a basket seller, and he said he would go adorn himself.
stories.turn: He threw himself from the roof, and Elijah caught him.
stories.outcome: When Rav Kahana blamed poverty, Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana sold palm baskets and was propositioned by a noblewoman. Saying he would get ready, he went up to the roof and jumped. Elijah caught him, complaining he had travelled four hundred parasangs, and when Rav Kahana said poverty had put him in this position, Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars.

stories.actor: A man in love with a woman
stories.event: A man pining for a woman he loved wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael for her.
stories.turn: He heard the teaching about Jacob's concern to be buried in the land.
stories.outcome: He stayed and suffered in the land until the day he died.
stories.summary: Ilfa told of a man who was suffering for love of a woman and wanted to go down from Eretz Yisrael. When he heard how much Jacob valued burial in the land, he remained and endured his suffering there until his death.

stories.actor: Shmuel
stories.event: As Shmuel was getting off a ferry, a man gave him a hand.
stories.turn: The man revealed he had a case to bring before Shmuel.
stories.outcome: Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging him.
stories.summary: Shmuel was crossing a river on a ferry and a man helped him out. Asked what he was doing there, the man said he had a lawsuit. Shmuel said he was now disqualified from judging the case.

stories.actor: Ameimar
stories.event: While Ameimar sat in judgment, a man removed a feather that landed on his head.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A feather fell on Ameimar's head as he judged, and a man brushed it off. When Ameimar learned the man had a case, he declared himself disqualified.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: A man covered spittle lying in front of Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: There was spittle in front of Mar Ukva and a man covered it. Learning the man had a case, Mar Ukva said he was disqualified from judging him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei and his sharecropper
stories.event: His sharecropper brought his weekly basket of fruit on Thursday instead of Friday, because he had a case in court.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and recused himself, yet while others judged he found himself thinking up arguments for the man.
stories.outcome: He exclaimed that if he was biased without even accepting, how much more are those who take bribes.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper always brought him fruit on Friday, but once came on Thursday because he had a lawsuit. Rabbi Yishmael refused the basket and appointed two other scholars to hear the case. Walking back and forth, he kept thinking of claims the sharecropper could make, and cried out: woe to those who take bribes, if I who took nothing, and only my own, feel this way.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, and the bride said she was still a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel tested two maidservants on a wine barrel, then the bride, and no scent diffused from her.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: A man told Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi that he found no blood, while his bride said she was still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel seated a virgin and a non-virgin maidservant over a wine barrel and found the scent rose only from the non-virgin; the bride was then tested and no scent rose, so he told the groom to accept her.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel the Elder
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, and the bride said her Dorketi family has neither menstrual nor hymenal blood.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel checked her relatives and found she was telling the truth.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take his acquisition and called him fortunate to marry into the Dorketi family.
stories.summary: A man complained to Rabban Gamliel the Elder that he found no blood. The bride said she came from the Dorketi family, whose women have no menstrual or hymenal blood. Rabban Gamliel investigated her female relatives, found it true, and told the groom to accept her, congratulating him.

stories.actor: A starving couple and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: During a drought, a groom told Rabbi he found no blood while the bride said she was still a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabbi saw their faces blackened by hunger and had them bathed, fed and given drink.
stories.outcome: The groom then found blood, and Rabbi told him to take his acquisition.
stories.summary: In years of famine a man told Rabbi that he found no blood, and his bride said she was a virgin. Seeing their faces darkened with hunger, Rabbi had them bathed, fed and given drink and sent into a room; this time the groom found blood. Rabbi told him to accept his bride and applied a verse about skin shriveled on bones.
